children.text:
Those are commercials? They are well done and work as commercials but I don't see any artistic intention (the way the parent comment was talking about) behind them, or happy mistakes as Bob Ross likes to call them.

> Taste is what makes an artist persist through struggling time and never giving up, even when the going gets rough and things aren't working out.

No actually, it's perseverance, skills and caring about making art. There are lots of art aficionados who have an impeccable taste in curation, but lack the skills or will to do anything. Then there are artists who have the skills and perseverance, but not the taste. It gets interesting when these two worlds combine.

With AI art, you commission an artificial artist, and if you have good taste, you can get good results if you curate well enough. But that road doesn't contain the struggle that defines art.

children.text:
> First off there was struggle for months before I got better results.

Yeah I just can't place that struggle into the same box, sorry. Especially when still after months your "taste" that came with the struggle includes you asking the AI for what to do next. But as you said you never claimed to be an artist, so that's on me for reading it that way.

Believe it or not my main point is not to bring your creativity down, and I'm sorry I probably said things that did. I'm happy that you get to express yourself and be creative, you do you.

I'm just hoping that all this discourse around this ends up creating new genres and terminology for art which we all can agree with. As with genres in music, there are cultural morals within those genres [1] and breaking those will cause a backlash within that genre. The same is happening with AI art. The cultural moral shared by many artists has been to go through the creative struggle, to not fake your skills, to have a mastery of a craft. AI art genre defies these expectations and that's why many, me included are offended by it. It's like faking your performance, where in pop music it's allowed, and in rock music it's frowned upon.

[1] https://youtu.be/R1QEV9euGAg?t=1644

But there was struggle, you just don't see it in the chat. First off there was struggle for months before I got better results. I had to find the techniques and understand how the AI works in order to get these results. In my view these images don't look like normal AI images but that's my opinion. And the image in the chat transcript took quite a bit of thinking in order to figure out what I wanted, even if it doesn't look like it in the transcript. Also I never claimed to be an artist just because of these images. I'm not sure what to call it. What I think is interesting about AI is to get as much as possible out of them to create something that looks decent that imo it does take some skill to do, but that's not the main point of it.

But I agree with you that creating art the manual way is for sure much harder than creating AI art. But that's not really the point as far as I'm concerned. With AI the skill is somewhere else, it's in the curation and the techniques one uses to accomplish the final product, which can be unique for each person if they really try to find their own techniques and their own way of doing things. There is a lot more room in the AI for personal expression that it looks like. I don't think you could recreate these images exactly how they look.

In this frame you are a commissioner or an art director, that's what those people do. Artist knows about the execution and does it.

Before AI with money you could've gone to any artist and commissioned to paint your ideas. And yes there would be lots of back and forth with the artist, the artist would create sketches for you that you then would comment on before letting the artist go on to create the finished piece.

In my other comment I said: "With AI art, you commission an artificial artist, and if you have good taste, you can get good results if you curate well enough. But that road doesn't contain the struggle that defines art.". I don't see any struggle in that chat with ChatGPT and for that reason none of those images make you an artist in my view. And trust me, I've tried Midjourney, ChatGPT, Gemini all the same, and none of that back and worth conversation struggle with those compare to the struggle of actually creating art yourself. You can't ask your brush where to place the text. You have to decide and live with your decision.

There is artistic intent, all of the ideas for the images are mine. If you read the whole transcript you will see that I came up with the laser on the bottle and the sheet in the background of the image (I didn't use the suggestions of the AI, but sometimes I do). I also came up with the main idea for the image through the inclusion of the reference image in the first prompt.

The same is true for all the other images. I spent a lot of time coming up with original compositions so that every image is unique from the other images. It's actually much harder than one thinks to come up with an interesting idea to have AI create.

But one thing you are hinting at is that yes, I leave the execution to the AI. I have the main idea and then I leave the exact composition to the AI because it's good at it. That's part of what makes AI interesting is that it can create good compositions and place things in a good way. I delegate as much as I can to the AI in fact. I don't see anything wrong with that, they're still partly my creations, and I don't think that takes away from what I did on my part, but we'll probably disagree on that I guess. This is the new way of working with AI for me is to delegate to the AI what it's good at, find its strongest sides and use those. In this case it's creating good balanced compositions, and emulating physics so that the laser looks realistic and so on.

Another thing that you don't see is that there was a lot of experimentation on the way to these images. It took me quite a while to get good results and that taught me what works and what doesn't.

Also looking at your transcript [1] it's obvious there's no artistic vision behind the images, just curation. An artist would like to place things exactly, would have an exact vision in mind. You're actually asking the LLM to place, because you don't even know what you want!

"can you put the bottle from the last image in the first image, but have the camera kind of top down, and make the scene dark. then have the pink lasers beaming through the room and have it hit the bottle in a neat way. make it a nice composition but still natural looking. also have the valentino logo and text "Born In Roma Intense" somewhere it fits"

"yeah thats good but what can we add to make the image more interesting"

"it looks great but for some reason i feel like somethging is missing but i dont know what"

Lmao. A good artist would know what to do to make the image more interesting. These images are not your art. They're the LLM's, it has made all the creative decisions.

[1] https://chatgpt.com/s/cx_6b079e225770819193b97c3e72de5076

I understand what you're saying and I agree with it to a certain extent, but I also think it's even more complicated than that.

I can only speak for myself but I know what it's like to create something from scratch and struggle. I created music and images for 20+ years the manual. I'll use music as an example. For me music making was always part curation. I'm looking for sounds that I want and I always had a vision / idea for what I wanted to create before I started the process. The thing is, nothing I ever did perfectly captured my intent. I experimented for hours and came up with techniques that resembled the idea I had and sounded good, and then I went with that.

I think it works like this for a lot of artists. A lot of music is discovered through experimentation with gear, melodies, synths etc, not intently created by the millisecond. It's a mix of discovery / compromise and intent. What differentiated any artist from any other was taste and vision. Taste is what makes an artist persist through struggling time and never giving up, even when the going gets rough and things aren't working out.

The other thing is that sometimes you discover a cool piece of technology like a synth, a drum machine or a plugin in Photoshop, and you discover that if you use it in a particular way, it creates a cool sound or a cool effect on an image. You didn't create that sound or effect purely by yourself, you discovered it in the tools and I think art has always been that way.

AI is a bit like all of the above. It's a cool piece of tech where you can discover techniques or things that normal usage doesn't uncover, and it's also curation in that you have a vision and you're trying to get that vision.

The only thing I can really appeal to are the original images I posted. I mean what do you see when you look at them? Do you see any intent or vision? Do you see anything unique or interesting in some way or does it just look like slop to you?

For the menu case specifically, the main problem (well besides them looking positively awful) is that the generated images just don't represent the product being sold at all. It should be a clear business-shattering false advertising issue but for some reason its tolerated everywhere.

source.text:
It sounds a little more like curation to me. You're exploring a (latent) space and finding pieces to share that are interesting or speak to you.

There's a lot to potentially discuss, but I'll try to train-of-thought some more relevant points into words.

Many creative arts aren't just about having an idea. Personally, I think ideas tend to be shockingly formless once you examine them up close, even ones that feel very concrete.

In things like visual arts, the "hard parts" aren't just throwaway. Every tiny stroke of a pencil, digital bush, etc. is a little decision that brings that longing formlessness into form. There are other important decisions during creation too; when you make a mistake do you incorporate it or throw it away? Each of these decisions may be easy or be difficult, but they're intentional.

While you you make those decisions, seeing the work materialize in front of you can cause the shape of the idea itself, your artistic vision, and even your tastes to change. The work is already influencing you and your idea before it's even finished.

When a person says something like, "I have an idea: a red building against a blue sky." they likely don't see every brick, or the shapes of the windows, or the way the strokes are laid. It's very easy for somebody else to show a picture of a red tower and infill most of the original idea their own. The original person's idea may be represented, but so are a lot of others. (Sometimes we even happily say, "Thanks. Here's $5 for filling that in.")

I feel that even very detailed prompts tend to only roughly approximate the level of intent expressed through the process of creating a piece. Intention isn't everything in art, but it's clearly an important something that's been a topic of discussion for a long time.

You also can't or won't prompt for certain things, so your end result will just never have those aspects. For example: An old discussion with a friend will never randomly cross your mind and causes you to accidentally lay a bunch of angry brush strokes in one place.

The formlessness of ideas also seems to make it relatively easy to give feedback. Again, real shape and decisions come when trying to turn that feedback to form.

If you just need a menu for your food truck or a picture of your grandchild with angel wings, maybe those rough prompts with a little refinement are serviceable. But, if your desire is to make some "art" and express your creativity or imagination, many potential viewers value things like intentionality (whether they realize it or not.) Outsourcing intent causes more weight to lean on an idea, so it better be a stellar idea, assuming it's even yours and not mostly the outsourcers--a question dangling over the viewer's mind.

Now compound that with generative AI making images a [mass-produced] commodity and causing viewers to be constantly bombarded with vague "ideas." How does an idea or a work stand out in that landscape? The level of intention becomes shorthand some viewers use to judge if they should pay attention to you. That makes it valuable to them and potentially an even more important differentiator than ever before.

[Edit: I also want to point out that a number of entities attempt to manipulate or trick viewers with these easy to produce images, so even if your intentions are good, audiences still develop filtering behaviors.]
